source: Li et al. (2024) Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach (Self-Route)
finding: Frozen LLMs, no fine-tuning. Giving the full long context beats chunk retrieval on average, but retrieval uses far fewer tokens. A cheap router (the model says 'unanswerable' from the retrieved chunks, then falls back to the full context) keeps most of the accuracy at lower cost.
numbers: Average over 9 datasets: Gemini-1.5-Pro long context (LC) 49.70, RAG 37.33, Self-Route 46.41 using 38.39% of the tokens. GPT-4o LC 48.67, RAG 32.60, Self-Route 48.89 using 61.40% of tokens. GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K window) LC 32.07, RAG 30.33, Self-Route 35.32. RAG and LC give identical predictions on 63% of queries. Self-Route cost is lowest at k=5 on average; k=1 best on extractive sets.
quote: LC consistently outperforms RAG in almost all settings
limits: Corpora are 7K to 100K+ token documents (Wikipedia, stories), not libraries of short items. Contriever retriever; Dragon gave a similar picture. Wikipedia sets may be partly memorised (leakage). Routing needs one extra call.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 1 in part: for a frozen model a full-context read wins on accuracy when it fits, retrieval wins on tokens, and a try-retrieval-first-then-widen policy gets most of both. Suggests a two-step lookup: top-5 first, widen only if the model says it cannot answer.

source: Yu, Xu, Akkiraju (2024) In Defense of RAG in the Era of Long-Context Language Models (OP-RAG)
finding: With a frozen 70B model, retrieving a modest amount of text beats reading the whole 117K-token context. Answer quality has an inverted U in the amount retrieved, and the peak moves later for bigger models.
numbers: EN.QA F1: Llama3.1-70B full context (117K tokens) 34.26; retrieval of 16K tokens 44.43, 24K 45.45, 48K 47.25. Gemini-1.5-Pro full context 43.08 at 196K tokens; GPT-4o 32.36. EN.MC accuracy: full 71.62; retrieval 16K 84.72, 24K 88.65, 48K 85.59. Peak context: Llama3.1-8B at 16K tokens; 70B at 48K (EN.QA) and 32K (EN.MC). Keeping retrieved chunks in original document order beat score order (38.40 vs 44.43 F1 at large k for 70B).
limits: Only two long-document QA sets (En.QA 351 questions, En.MC 224). Chunk size fixed at 128 tokens. The order-preserving trick needs ordered source text; for a library of independent items it may not apply. Gemini and GPT-4o rows are copied from another paper.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 2: for a frozen LLM reader the optimum is a few thousand to tens of thousands of tokens (125 to 375 chunks of 128 tokens), then quality declines. The peak depends on model size, so tune k per model.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) The Power of Noise: Redefining Retrieval for RAG Systems
finding: Distractors are documents that score high on retrieval but do not hold the answer. Adding one next to the gold document cuts accuracy sharply, and accuracy keeps falling as distractors are added. Random unrelated documents hurt much less and sometimes helped when placed next to the query.
numbers: NQ-open, gold document known, 10K training queries. Llama2 gold-only 0.5642; 1 distractor 0.4586; 2 distractors 0.3455; 4 -> 0.2745; 8 -> 0.2643; 18 -> 0.2348 (far setting). Text: drops of up to 0.38 (-67%) across LLMs, and one distractor alone costs up to 0.24 (-25%). Closed-book Llama2 is 0.1123, so even many distractors leave it above closed-book. Random documents (near setting): Llama2 rose from 0.5642 to 0.5859 with 14 random documents (abstract claims up to 35% gain); not always significant.
limits: Models are Llama2, MPT, Phi-2, Falcon: small and old, 2048-token limit, NQ only. The random-document gain is odd and may be an attention or format effect; do not rely on it. Distractors are defined by retrieval score, so they are hard negatives.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 answered with effect sizes: near-miss library items (high similarity but not useful) are the harm, not random ones. A retriever returning similar-looking but wrong subgoals is worse than a weaker one. Put the best item nearest the question.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context (GSM-IC)
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to grade-school maths word problems breaks reasoning for code-davinci-002 and text-davinci-003. Self-consistency and an 'ignore irrelevant information' instruction help a little; showing examples that contain irrelevant text helps more.
numbers: Of the problems the baseline solves, no more than 18% are solved for every kind of irrelevant sentence (chain-of-thought prompts). The paper's text says self-consistency raises recall on GSM-IC for all prompting methods and that the share of correct answers reachable among samples is as high as 99.7%. Table 3 per-method values were not transcribed. Changing the numbers in the distractor does little; overlap of topic with the problem matters most.
limits: GPT-3 era models, one task type. Macro accuracy counts a base problem only if all variants are right, a strict view. Modern models are more robust, but d03 and d06 show the effect persists with retrieved text.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule not to pad the working context with loosely related subgoals. If it must be done, include examples that show ignoring irrelevant items, and use consistency voting.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Multi-document QA with 10, 20 or 30 retrieved documents. Accuracy is highest when the answer document is first or last and falls in the middle. With 20 and 30 documents the worst case is below having no document. Reader accuracy flattens long before retrieval recall does.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo: closed-book 56.1%, oracle (only the gold document) 88.3%. Drop of more than 20% when the gold document sits in the middle; at 20 and 30 documents the worst case is below closed-book. Text: using more than 20 retrieved documents gave only marginal gains.
limits: Models of 2023 (GPT-3.5, Claude-1.3, MPT-30B, LongChat); newer models are more position-robust (see d06). NQ-open Wikipedia only.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 anchor in QA: oracle minus closed-book is 32 points for GPT-3.5, and 20 retrieved documents can give negative gain. Gap 2: for an LLM reader the useful number of retrieved items is below about 20, and position in the prompt matters.

source: Jin, Yoon, Han, Arik (2024) Long-Context LLMs Meet RAG: Overcoming Challenges for Long Inputs in RAG
finding: On 2024 long-context models, more retrieved passages first help then hurt. The cause is hard negatives, and a stronger retriever gives harder negatives. Reordering and robustness fine-tuning mitigate it.
numbers: NQ: with the strong e5 retriever (recall@40 0.90) accuracy rises then falls sharply or plateaus for all 4 LLMs; with BM25 (recall@40 0.73) accuracy keeps rising or dips slightly. Controlled test: one gold passage plus n hard negatives; accuracy falls as n grows for all LLMs; e5 negatives hurt more than BM25 or random negatives; Gemini-1.5-Pro is robust to random negatives but not to hard ones. Reordering helps only at large passage counts.
limits: Results read from figures, so exact peak positions were not recorded. Datasets NQ and PopQA. Training fixes use Gemma-2-9B and Mistral-Nemo-12B.
agent_relevance: Independent of d03 and same direction. A better retriever is not automatically a better pipeline; set k after choosing the retriever and compare retrievers at their own best k, not at a fixed k.

source: Yoran, Wolfson, Ram, Berant (2023) Making Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Robust to Irrelevant Context
finding: Retrieval hurts on some multi-hop tasks even with a strong retriever; random context dramatically lowers accuracy on all five datasets. An NLI filter removes the harm but also drops useful passages. Fine-tuning on a mix of relevant and irrelevant context with about 1,000 examples gives robustness.
numbers: Five open-domain QA sets (four multi-hop). Top-1 Google search context lowers accuracy on StrategyQA and Fermi versus no retrieval. Per-dataset deltas are in the paper tables 2 and 3 (Llama-2-13B) and were not transcribed here. The abstract states that 1,000 examples suffice to train robustness.
limits: Needs fine-tuning, which our agent does not do. Only the failure pattern and the NLI-filter baseline transfer (an entailment check can be done by prompting). Numeric effect sizes not recorded.
agent_relevance: A cheap filter step (does this retrieved item bear on the goal?) prevents harm but costs recall; this is the same trade-off as a score threshold.

source: Su et al. (2024) BRIGHT: A Realistic and Challenging Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval (ICLR 2025)
finding: Where relevance needs reasoning (maths, code, science), standard retrievers score low. Having an LLM first write reasoning steps and using that as the query roughly doubles BM25. Reranking by a strong LLM adds more. Retrieval closes under half of the oracle gap in end-to-end QA.
numbers: Best retriever 24.3 nDCG@10 on average; a top MTEB model scores 59.0 on BEIR but 18.3 on BRIGHT. BM25 average 14.5 on original queries vs 27.0 with GPT-4 reasoning-step queries (Table 38); Claude-written 26.8. Reranking BM25 top-100 with GPT-4 at k=10 lifted 14.3 to 17.4. QA with Claude-3.5-Sonnet on StackExchange: no retrieval 77.7, BM25 78.3, SBERT 79.0, Qwen embedding 79.6, oracle documents 81.8 (best retriever +1.9 of a +4.1 oracle gap, 46%).
limits: Retrieved items are web documents, not subgoals. The tokens spent on reasoning rewrites are not counted against any budget. QA judged by Claude-3.5-Sonnet (self-evaluation).
agent_relevance: Gaps 3, 7, 9. BM25 plus an LLM-written reasoning query beats dense retrieval on the raw query, so lexical match is enough if the query is rewritten first. An oracle gap exists but even the best retriever closes under half of it.

source: Shao et al. (2025) ReasonIR: Training Retrievers for Reasoning Tasks
finding: A bi-encoder trained on synthetic reasoning queries plus synthetic hard negatives. Longer rewritten queries help it where other retrievers plateau. A compute estimate shows rewriting plus a bi-encoder costs far less than an LLM reranker at similar accuracy.
numbers: BRIGHT nDCG@10: 24.4 on original queries, 29.9 with GPT-4 rewritten queries, 36.9 with an LLM reranker added. Ablation (Llama3.1-8B base, no rewriting): public data only 19.6, plus HQ 20.9, plus VL 23.2, plus HQ+VL 24.4; with rewriting HQ+VL 28.5. Easy synthetic queries (EQ) added nothing. Rewriting from 64 to 256 tokens helps ReasonIR while other retrievers plateau. Beats Rank1-32B with over 200 times less test-time compute (their FLOPs estimate). RAG: MMLU +6.4% and GPQA +22.6% relative to closed-book.
limits: Authors' own FLOPs estimate. The comparison is not equal-token against reading more context. One benchmark (BRIGHT). 8B retriever.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 10: reasoning rewriting is a cheap add (a few hundred tokens per query) that pays more per FLOP than LLM reranking. Hard negatives that look relevant but are not are what make the selector learn; easy negatives did not help.

source: Weller et al. (2025) Rank1: Test-Time Compute for Reranking in Information Retrieval
finding: A reranker that writes a reasoning chain before judging relevance. The chain gives the gain; forcing longer thinking (budget forcing) did not help.
numbers: BRIGHT average nDCG@10: Rank1-7B 27.5 vs 17.5 for the same model trained without reasoning chains and 13.9 for RankLLaMA-7B. Reasoning chains in the 600,000-example training set were all under 1,000 tokens. Budget forcing from s1 did not improve and slightly hurt in limited tests.
limits: Reranker over BM25 top-100 of GPT-4o CoT rewritten queries (so rewriting cost is already inside). Distilled from R1 on MS MARCO. Up to 1,000 output tokens per document, so reranking 100 candidates costs up to 100K output tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the reasoning is paid in tokens per candidate. For a subgoal library, rerank only the top 5 to 10 with a cap of a few hundred tokens each. The paper does not charge this against a budget.

source: Wang et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover: Neural Theorem Proving with Growing Libraries
finding: A frozen ChatGPT/GPT-4 prover in Isabelle that adds each proven lemma to a vector-store skill library during the run and retrieves from it. The library grows while the run goes on, which is our setting.
numbers: miniF2F-valid 57.0% and test 50.0% with 100 attempts. Ablation at 50 attempts on valid: with growing library 50.4%, without library 47.1% (+3.3 points). The gap starts near zero when the library is empty and widens as skills are added. Of 135 valid problems proved, 24% used retrieved skills; of those, 51% reused a skill directly and 49% wrote a new lemma by imitation. Cost about 300 USD per 100-attempt experiment.
limits: Single ablation, 50 attempts, one run; 3.3 points is a handful of the 244 problems, so error bars matter. Skills retrieved by LLM-written request with OpenAI ada embeddings, not by goal state. miniF2F is easy and many problems need no skill.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 4: with a frozen LLM a library that grows during the run helps, and the benefit grows with library size; no retraining was needed for new items. Most solved problems did not need retrieval, so measure on the hard slice.

source: Thompson et al. (2025) Rango: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Proving for Automated Software Verification
finding: Coq proof synthesis with retrieval at every proof step. It retrieves similar earlier proofs keyed by the current proof state (BM25) and lemmas. Retrieving earlier proofs matters far more than retrieving lemmas, and sparse beats dense.
numbers: CoqStoq: 2,226 projects, 196,929 theorems; Rango proves 32.0%. Ablation on 500 theorems: Rango 150 (30.0%), without lemma retriever 145 (29.0%), without proof retriever 102 (20.4%), with neither 93 (18.6%). Proof retriever worth +47%, lemma retriever +3%. BM25 beat CodeBERT dense retrieval by 46% and TF-IDF by 1%. Held-out-project test: variants without proof retrieval gained 26% and 43% when project files were in the training weights; with proof retrieval only 15% and 11%. Rollout search 30.0% vs best-first 28.4% and 25.0%.
limits: Fine-tuned LLM, not frozen. Proof states compared by word counts. Possible pretraining contamination for older projects (authors added two post-cutoff projects).
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 4: keying retrieval on the current goal state and returning earlier solved goals with their solutions worked best, and it substitutes for project knowledge in the weights. This is close to our subgoal library: store goal plus solution, retrieve by goal text with lexical match.

source: Lu et al. (2026) Lean Finder: Semantic Search for Mathlib That Understands User Intents (ICLR 2026)
finding: Embedding retriever fine-tuned on synthetic user queries and proof states and aligned to a preference signal. Retrieval from a raw proof state is much harder than from a natural-language query, and adding a plain-language description of the state roughly triples top-1 recall.
numbers: Recall@1/5/10 (MRR): informalized statements 64.2/88.9/93.3 (0.75) vs Lean Search 49.2/76.5/82.5 (0.61) vs GPT-4o name match 14.8/20.9/22.6. Synthetic user queries 54.4/84.4/91.4 (0.68). Proof states: augmented with NL description 24.6/56.8/67.9 (0.40) vs raw state 8.3/30.1/40.0 (0.19); baselines Lean State Search 4.99/27.7/39.6, Real Prover Search 8.0/29.0/39.2; Qwen3-Embedding-8B 8.0/26.1/34.7 on augmented. Users ranked Lean Finder top-3 in 81.6% of votes vs 56.9% Lean Search and 54.1% GPT-4o (5 participants, 128 queries). Downstream gains small (see K17).
limits: Test sets are the authors' own synthetic distribution, so these are not independent replications. User study tiny. The GPT-4o baseline writes names from memory.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 6: storing a short natural-language gloss with each subgoal makes retrieval from state-like text several times better at rank 1. Gap 6 stays open: the numbers are self-reported on the authors' benchmark.

source: Gan and Sun (2025) RAG-MCP: Mitigating Prompt Bloat in LLM Tool Selection via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
finding: Frozen LLM choosing among many tool descriptions. Pasting all descriptions into the prompt wrecks selection; retrieving the top tool first gives about three times the accuracy at about half the prompt tokens.
numbers: MCPBench web-search subset, qwen-max-0125, 20 trials per method, success = more than 10 of 20 correct. Accuracy: retrieval 43.13%, keyword pre-filter 18.20%, all descriptions in prompt 13.62%. Average prompt tokens 1,084 vs 1,646 vs 2,134; completion tokens 78 vs 24 vs 162. Stress test with N from 1 to 11,100 servers (distractors from over 4,400 real servers): success above 90% below position 30, patchy from 31 to 70, mostly failing beyond about 100.
limits: Short single-domain preprint, not peer reviewed; judged by DeepSeek-v3; the stress-test text and figure are ambiguous about which method is plotted. Only the top-1 tool is injected.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a measured crossover for a frozen LLM, in the tens up to about 100 library items, beyond which putting everything in the prompt fails. The token saving is only about half here because the prompt is small anyway.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models (skill library)
finding: A frozen GPT-4 agent stores working code skills in a library and retrieves the top 5 by embedding of the task and plan. Removing the library makes later progress plateau and slows unseen tasks.
numbers: Skill retrieval accuracy over 309 samples: top-1 80.2 +/- 3.0, top-2 89.3, top-3 93.2, top-4 95.2, top-5 96.5 +/- 0.3. Zero-shot unseen tasks (3 trials each): with library 19, 18, 21, 18 prompting iterations, 3/3 successes on all four; without library 36 (2/3), 30 (3/3), 27 (3/3), 26 (3/3); AutoGPT with Voyager's library succeeded in 1/3, 1/3, 0/3 and 2/3 trials.
limits: Minecraft code generation; three trials per task; GPT-4 snapshot of March 2023. Retrieval hits judged by hand-set labels.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 4: top-5 from a growing library of verified skills works with a frozen model at 96.5% recall at 5. The library also transfers to another agent, which fits sharing a subgoal library.

source: Moreira et al. (2024) NV-Retriever: Improving text embedding models with effective hard-negative mining
finding: Which negatives to train a selector on matters: the strongest-looking negatives are often unlabeled positives. Mining negatives that stay below a margin of the positive score fixes this.
numbers: Fine-tuned e5-large-unsupervised, average NDCG@10 on NQ, HotpotQA and FiQA: negatives mined with BM25 0.5002, random 0.5248, best teacher (e5-mistral-7b) 0.5810. Mining methods at best setting: naive top-k 0.5407, top-k shifted by 10 0.569, TopK-Abs 0.7 0.5759, TopK-MarginPos 0.05 0.583, TopK-PercPos 95% 0.5856. Accuracy falls when negatives score above about 95% of the positive score. Top-4 negatives from four teacher models agree under 30% (Jaccard).
limits: Web-QA text retrieval with large training sets; not a few-example setting. No LLM reader involved.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: when choosing near-miss negatives for calibration, take items that are similar but score under about 95% of the true match, skip the top few ranks (often unlabeled positives), and use a different model's ranking than the one being tuned.

source: Li, Cao, Ma, Sun (2024) Long Context vs. RAG for LLMs: An Evaluation and Revisits
finding: Re-runs the long-context versus RAG debate after filtering questions the model can answer without context. Long context wins overall, especially on Wikipedia and stories; RAG wins on fragmented, dialogue and general-question settings. Explains the conflict among earlier studies by context relevance and corpus type.
numbers: Across 12 datasets after filtering: LC correct on 56.3% of questions, RAG 49.0%. LC alone correct on more than 2,000 questions, RAG alone on about 1,300. Summarization-based retrieval roughly matched LC; chunk retrieval lagged. Table 1 lists 9 earlier studies with conflicting verdicts.
limits: Mixed benchmark of long documents; questions answerable from memory removed. Retrieval is chunk-based for documents, not for libraries of separate items.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: no single winner; it depends on whether the needed facts sit together (favours a full read) or are scattered and short (favours retrieval). A subgoal library is the scattered case.
